title: What do Japanese restaurants and food businesses need for HACCP and a food hygiene manager?
seoTitle: Japan HACCP and food hygiene manager
description: Japan's Food Sanitation Act: HACCP based hygiene control for all food businesses since June 2021, the food hygiene manager role, and staff training duties.
shortAnswer: Under Japan's Food Sanitation Act as amended in 2018, almost every food business operator has had to implement HACCP based hygiene control since June 1, 2021, with a simplified approach for small operators. The Enforcement Regulation also requires operators to appoint a food hygiene manager (shokuhin eisei sekininsha), qualified by profession or by a prefectural course, and to train food handlers and periodically verify that training works.
keyTakeaways: The Act to Partially Amend the Food Sanitation Act (Act No. 46 of 2018) was promulgated on June 13, 2018, and MHLW says HACCP based hygiene control applies, in principle, to all food business operators from June 1, 2021.

Article 51 of the Food Sanitation Act requires operators to follow MHLW ordinance standards for general hygiene and for control of critical processes; small operators follow an approach suited to their food.
Article 66-4 of the Enforcement Regulation treats establishments with fewer than 50 food handling staff as small scale, allowing the simplified approach using sector guidance documents.
Appended Table 17, item 1 requires operators to appoint a food hygiene manager, who must be a qualifying professional or have completed a course run or approved by the prefecture.
Appended Table 17, item 13 requires education for food handlers, safe chemical handling training, and periodic verification of training effectiveness.
jurisdiction: Japan: Food Sanitation Act (Act No. 233 of 1947) and Ordinance for Enforcement of the Food Sanitation Act (Ministry of Health and Welfare Ordinance No. 23 of 1948)
regulator: Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW) sets the hygiene control standards; prefectures, designated cities and special wards license, inspect and run food hygiene manager courses
appliesTo: Restaurants, cafes and other licensed or notified food businesses
Food manufacturers and processors, including bakeries and prepared food makers
Food retailers, other than those exempted as low public health impact
Non-commercial group feeding facilities such as schools and hospitals, unless they serve fewer than about 20 meals per sitting
Food hygiene managers (shokuhin eisei sekininsha) and all food handling staff

sections.heading: When did HACCP become mandatory in Japan, and for whom?

blocks.text: HACCP based hygiene control has applied, in principle, to all food business operators in Japan since June 1, 2021. The [MHLW HACCP page](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/stf/seisakunitsuite/bunya/kenkou_iryou/shokuhin/haccp/index.html) states this directly, following the 2018 amendment of the Food Sanitation Act, which MHLW's [amendment overview](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/stf/seisakunitsuite/bunya/0000197196.html) records as promulgated on June 13, 2018.

MHLW lists exclusions. Agricultural and fishery harvesting is outside the scheme. Four lower risk business types must maintain general hygiene control but need not implement HACCP based control: importers of food or additives, businesses that only store or transport food (excluding frozen and refrigerated warehousing), sellers of packaged food that does not spoil at ambient temperature, and importers or sellers of utensils and packaging. Non-commercial group feeding facilities such as schools and hospitals are in scope, but those serving fewer than about 20 meals per sitting do not need to comply.

The amendment also abolished the older comprehensive sanitation management approval system on June 1, 2020, so the HACCP requirement now runs through the general Article 51 standards rather than a voluntary approval route.

sections.heading: What is the difference between the two HACCP tiers?

blocks.text: Larger operators follow full HACCP based control under Appended Table 18 of the Enforcement Regulation; small operators may follow an approach suited to the characteristics of the food they handle. Article 51(1)(ii) of the [Food Sanitation Act](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/322AC0000000233) creates the split, and the Enforcement Regulation defines who is small.

blocks.caption: Who may use the simplified approach (Enforcement Regulation, Articles 66-3 and 66-4, as at November 2026)
head: Category
Examples in the Regulation
Applicable standard
rows: Restaurants, cafes, school and hospital facilities, cooking vending machines, short shelf life bread makers, prepared food (sozai) makers
Approach suited to food characteristics, using sector guidance
Businesses that divide and package food for sale
Any manufacturing, processing, storage, sales or handling site with fewer than 50 food handling staff
Approach suited to food characteristics, for those sites only
Sites with 50 or more food handling staff, for example
Full HACCP principles in Appended Table 18

blocks.text: MHLW publishes sector guidance documents prepared by food industry associations for the simplified approach. An operator with both a large and a small site applies the simplified standard only to the small site, under the proviso in Article 66-4(ii).

sections.heading: What must every food business operator do under Article 66-2?

blocks.text: Every operator in scope must write a hygiene control plan and make it known to staff, prepare procedures where needed, keep records, and verify and review the plan. Article 66-2(3) of the [Enforcement Regulation](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/323M40000100023) sets these four steps.

items: Prepare a hygiene control plan for facility hygiene and food handling, and ensure it is thoroughly communicated to food handlers and other relevant people.
Prepare procedure documents where needed, such as for cleaning, washing, disinfection and food handling.
Record and keep records of how hygiene control was carried out, with a retention period set reasonably by reference to how long the food takes to be used or consumed.
Verify the effectiveness of the plan and procedures and revise them as needed.

blocks.text: For the lower risk business types in Article 66-2(4), the plan and records are required only "as necessary." Article 51(3) of the Act also allows prefectures to add local ordinance requirements so long as they do not conflict with the national standards, so local rules should be checked for each site.

sections.heading: Who must appoint a food hygiene manager, and who qualifies?

blocks.text: Operators subject to Article 51 must appoint a food hygiene manager (食品衛生責任者, shokuhin eisei sekininsha) under Appended Table 17, item 1 of the Enforcement Regulation, unless they are one of the lower risk business types in Article 66-2(4). The name, qualification type and course attended are also listed among the details given when applying for a business license.

blocks.caption: Food hygiene manager qualification routes (Appended Table 17, item 1(ro))
head: Route
Who qualifies
rows: A person meeting the qualification requirements for a food sanitation inspector (Article 30) or food sanitation supervisor (Article 48) under the Act
Licensed cooks (chorishi), confectionery hygienists, dietitians, registered dietitians, ship cooks, and designated slaughterhouse and poultry processing hygiene managers
A person who has completed a course run by the prefectural governor (or equivalent), or a course the governor recognizes as appropriate

blocks.text: A food sanitation supervisor appointed under Article 48 for specified manufacturing, such as dairy products, may also serve as the food hygiene manager. Article 48 is a separate, stricter role requiring a full time supervisor per facility for those products.

sections.heading: What ongoing training duties apply to the manager and staff?

blocks.text: For licensed businesses, the food hygiene manager must periodically attend courses run or recognized by the prefecture to keep up with new food hygiene knowledge, and must carry out hygiene control under the operator's instructions. The operator must respect the manager's opinions, and the manager should give the operator necessary advice.

blocks.title: Primary text: Enforcement Regulation, Appended Table 17, item 13 (education and training), translated
blocks.text: Provide food handlers with the education needed for hygiene control; provide those who handle chemicals with education and training so they can handle the chemicals safely; and periodically verify the effectiveness of that education and training, revising its content as necessary.

Item 13 is notable because it requires verification of training effectiveness, not just delivery. That aligns closely with the HACCP verification step and is a good fit for structured [competency assessment](/glossary/competency-assessment) rather than attendance records alone.

sections.heading: How can a Japanese food business map these duties to evidence?

blocks.text: A business can map each duty to the role, the frequency and the record a health center inspector would expect. The table is an illustrative template, not an MHLW form.

blocks.caption: Illustrative Food Sanitation Act obligation map

rows: Hygiene control plan communicated to staff (Art 66-2(3)(i))

blocks.text: Operators with sites in several prefectures should record each prefecture's course and refresher rules separately. See [how to build a training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix) and [how to evidence training effectiveness to a regulator](/guides/how-to-evidence-training-effectiveness-to-a-regulator). Workplace safety training for the same staff is covered under the [Industrial Safety and Health Act](/regulations/japan-industrial-safety-and-health-act-training).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry can link each step of a site's hygiene control plan to defined learning outcomes and assessment points, so the item 13 requirement to verify training effectiveness produces evidence tied to the plan version in force. See [operational procedure programs](/programs/operational-procedures).

faqs.q: Does a small restaurant in Japan need HACCP?
faqs.a: Yes, in a simplified form. Restaurants are listed in Article 66-3 of the Enforcement Regulation among operators who follow an approach suited to the characteristics of their food, using sector guidance documents published through MHLW. They still need a hygiene control plan, records and periodic review.

faqs.q: Can a licensed cook (chorishi) be the food hygiene manager?
faqs.a: Yes. Appended Table 17, item 1 lists licensed cooks, confectionery hygienists, dietitians and registered dietitians among those who qualify without attending the prefectural course. Others qualify by completing a course run or recognized by the prefectural governor.

faqs.q: Does the food hygiene manager need refresher training?
faqs.a: For businesses that require a license under Article 54, Appended Table 17 says the manager must periodically attend courses run or recognized by the prefecture to learn new food hygiene knowledge. The interval is not fixed nationally, so the local prefecture's arrangements apply.

faqs.q: How long must HACCP records be kept in Japan?
faqs.a: The Enforcement Regulation does not set a single period. Article 66-2(3)(iii) says the retention period should be set reasonably by reference to how long the food or additive takes to be used or consumed. A product eaten the same day and a product with a long shelf life will therefore justify different retention periods.

factCheck.claim: From June 1, 2021 (令和3年6月1日), in principle all food business operators implement HACCP based hygiene control; exclusions for agricultural and fishery harvesting, four low impact business types, and group feeding facilities under about 20 meals per sitting; comprehensive sanitation management approval abolished June 1, 2020.
Act to Partially Amend the Food Sanitation Act etc. (Act No. 46 of 2018) promulgated June 13, 2018; small operators may use simplified approach with MHLW published guidance.

Food Sanitation Act Article 51(1): MHLW ordinance standards for (i) general hygiene and (ii) control of critical processes, with small operators following an approach suited to food characteristics; 51(2) operators must comply; 51(3) prefectural ordinances; Article 48 food sanitation supervisor for specified manufacturing.

Enforcement Regulation Art 66-2: Table 17 and Table 18 standards; plan, procedures, records (retention set reasonably), verification; low risk types apply plan and records as necessary. Art 66-3 and 66-4: restaurants and similar, repackagers, establishments with fewer than 50 food handling staff.

Appended Table 17 item 1: operators appoint 食品衛生責任者; qualifications (inspector or Article 48 supervisor requirements; cooks, confectionery hygienists, dietitians etc.; prefectural course); duties including periodic course attendance for Article 54 licensed businesses; operator respects manager's opinions; Article 48 supervisor may double as manager.
Appended Table 17 item 13: education for food handlers, chemical handling training, periodic verification of training effectiveness and revision.
